figures.title: Dataset and train/test split
figures.text: 4,750 samples: 950 real landslide days and 3,800 non-landslide days (the same places on other days, and other places on the same day). Training 2007–2016 (3,375 samples), test 2017–2024 (1,375 samples, never seen in training).

figures.title: Training vs validation loss
figures.text: One blue/orange pair per internal fold (5 folds). Training stops automatically (early stopping, dot) when the validation loss stops improving, which prevents over-fitting.

figures.title: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC: training vs test
figures.text: Test accuracy 85.7% vs training 89.4%; the small gap means the model generalises to years it never saw. Red line: a useless model that always says 'no landslide' would already score 71% accuracy, so recall and ROC-AUC matter more than accuracy here. Recall is lower on training because landslides are 16% of training samples vs 29% of test samples.

figures.title: Confusion matrix (test set)
figures.text: Model at 50%: 242 landslides caught, 156 missed, 41 false alarms, 936 correct 'no alarm'. Percentages are per actual class (row).

figures.title: ROC curve
figures.text: How many landslides are caught (up) for each false-alarm rate (right) as the alarm level is moved. Closer to the top-left corner is better; the area under the curve (AUC) summarises it.

figures.title: Precision–recall curve
figures.text: For rare events this is stricter than ROC: it shows what share of alarms were real landslides at each level of recall.

figures.title: Calibration and confidence distribution
figures.text: Left: dots on the dashed line mean the confidence can be read as a probability. Above the line at the high end (it said 75%, 99% were landslides): on the test years the model is cautious, not over-confident, partly because landslides are a larger share of the test samples (29%) than of the training samples (16%). Right: real landslide days (red) get high confidence, other days (grey) mostly low.

figures.title: Feature importance
figures.text: How much the test ROC-AUC falls when inputs are randomly shuffled. Left: whole groups shuffled together (the fair comparison). Right: one input at a time; single rain windows look small because the other nine rain windows carry almost the same information.

figures.title: Choosing the alarm level
figures.text: A lower alarm level catches more landslides (recall) but raises more false alarms. The best F1 score on the test set is at about 25%.

figures.title: Learning curve
figures.text: With more training data the training score falls (0.969 → 0.929) and the test score stays about the same (0.884 → 0.895): the gap between them narrows, i.e. less over-fitting. Better (more precisely dated and located) records would help more than simply more of the same.

figures.title: Spatial test (unseen states)
figures.text: Each bar: the model is trained without these states and tested on them, to check it works in places it has never seen.
